items.question: How did you decide that moving from chip design to AI at Google was the right next step in 2010?
items.object: The decision to move from chip design to AI at Google in 2010
items.answer: Around 2010, I decided chip design was getting slow. Most of the interesting development was not happening there, and I started to think about what would be the next step for me. I thought AI would take off. That was my prediction in 2010, when for most people it was not obvious, but I thought this would be happening soon. I considered which company was the best place to join, and thought Google had the most data and the most talent in that direction. I joined Google in 2010.

I considered which company was the best place to join, and thought Google had the most data and the most talent in that direction. I joined Google in 2010.

items.question: How do you assess the usefulness of the Inception neural network you designed?
items.answer: The network I designed, Inception, was very useful back then, when there were mostly CPUs used in the data centers, because the network was much more efficient than AlexNet on CPU architectures. It's still used in embedded systems quite a bit, I hear from people. It's not the highest quality network, but it's one of the most efficient for those purposes.

items.question: How has your view of reasoning as the next big thing in AI shaped the research you chose to pursue?
items.object: Reasoning and autoformalization as directions for AI research
items.answer: I worked on computer vision until it became very crowded, and I was thinking, okay, now it's time to do the real deal and do reasoning, which back then was not really in progress. It took six or seven more years before people started to focus on reasoning. I thought that would be the next big thing, so let's do reasoning with AI. I started a team at Google on what was called informal, the idea of connecting formal and informal reasoning via neural networks. That's what I worked on until 2022, when we wanted to scale it up dramatically and tried to get resources for it at Google. They said this work is very important, they would come back to us in half a year, and at some point that didn't work, so let's start a company. We talked to several people trying to get funding, and at some point it turned out Elon also wanted to start an AI company. We went there, and that's where xAI started. After one and a half years I found that xAI didn't want to focus. They wanted to focus on informal reasoning, which was not my main interest. I thought, let's switch gears again. That was when I joined Morph this year, and we started to work on the actual autoformalization idea again, formalizing all of mathematics. We made some progress on that.

items.question: How do you understand the relationship between formal mathematics and formal logic?
items.object: The relationship between formal mathematics, formal logic, and theorem provers
items.answer: I see a very close relationship. Formal math is logic turned into a program. They use the same logic as formal logic uses. Formal logic is basically a procedure described informally so humans could check on paper whether something is correct in theory. Typically you need thousands of steps even to prove a simple theorem like the Pythagorean theorem. You need tens of thousands of steps, actually, and humans cannot do it by hand, but a computer can easily do it. Formal logic can be a specification of a computer chip, and when you implement an abstract theorem prover, that's like implementing a chip, taping it out, and then being able to run it at high speed. That's the connection between formal logic and theorem provers.

items.question: How do you compare theorem-proving systems in terms of their convenience for human mathematicians?
items.object: Lean and the usability of different theorem-proving systems
items.answer: There are a lot of formal logics people use, several different ones. There's first-order logic, the more classical one that people use. There are theorem provers based on that, but they're very inconvenient for humans to use. Then there are higher-order logic systems, and nowadays a special higher-order logic, dependent type-based prover Lean, is the most convenient for human mathematicians to use, in my view.
quotes: There are a lot of formal logics people use, several different ones. There's first-order logic, the more classical one that people use. items.question: Why do you prefer the term superintelligence to AGI when describing your objectives for AI?
items.object: Superintelligence as a term and objective compared with AGI
items.answer: To clarify my terminology, I don't really use AGI ever because that's a very overloaded term and everybody means something different by it. I use superintelligence as a word for domain-specific intelligence that exceeds human abilities by a large margin. That's why I prefer superintelligence: you can say mathematical superintelligence means it's a vastly better mathematician than any human. That's a much more quantifiable objective term, in my opinion. AGI is very hard to tell because the coverage of what is an AGI, what AGI really covers, is very unclear to me, and that's why I don't use that term. If I say it's superintelligent in this respect, like it can detect certain objects better than a human, I think that's clear what it means, or at least you can develop a benchmark for it. That's why I prefer that.

items.question: Why do you prefer objectively testable notions when discussing intelligence?
items.answer: I prefer notions that I can objectively test. Basically, if I say that I can tell, is it X or is it not X? If X is an ocean, to me that's a notion quantified by a fuzzy set, a set that is not clearly specified what it is. It's basically an unfalsifiable statement. That's why I don't prefer it.

items.question: How broadly do you see mathematical reasoning covering the tasks an intelligent agent might face?
items.object: Mathematical reasoning as a foundation for general reasoning
items.answer: I believe that an agent that can reason about mathematics would cover 99% of all the reasoning tasks that anybody can come up with. Mathematics is harder to apply, but for me mathematics is a much wider notion than most people use. For me, mathematical logic would cover almost everything, but I don't want to make that kind of statement because I don't want to overhype it. I really believe in that.

items.question: How do you understand the role of mathematics in enabling AI to capture aspects of reality?
items.object: Mathematics as a way for AI to capture aspects of reality
items.answer: I don't say necessarily that everything needs to be formally specified and then formally processed and translated back. That's a big part of it. If you get better and better understanding of certain aspects of reality, at some point you can capture those aspects mathematically. What I mean by mathematically is not necessarily the same notion of mathematical that most people think. It's not like, okay, give a few simple formulas or a theory of everything. Mathematics can also be an extremely complicated probability distribution. You can make statements and then do bounds on that distribution. What AI does is represent probability distributions. Today's AI's neural networks represent them using thousands of matrices, but for mathematics it's just a few. AI is also mathematics, essentially; it's a bunch of matrix multiplications and extra functions, and it captures probability distributions very mathematically. We can make mathematical statements about those, so I believe mathematics can capture much more than what we think it can. Humans are not very good at math, so we cannot use math as much as we would need to get really good, but AI will not have that constraint. That's the point here.

items.question: Why do you focus on formal verification rather than approximating reality with neural networks without verification?
items.object: Formal verification as an AI research direction
items.answer: I think AI research has a lot of very useful paths. One path is approximating reality with neural networks without any verification. That's still an extremely useful and important agenda, and most people focus on it. That's not my focus, because everybody else is doing it. I'm convinced formal verification will gain importance in the next few years.

items.question: Why do you see formal verification as a safer safeguard against AI subversion than having another AI check its work?
items.object: Formal verification as a safeguard against AI subversion
items.answer: I believe AI needs to be somehow kept in check as we go on, because AI is getting more powerful and we don't exactly know what it does. We want to create safeguards for AI not subverting what we're asking from it. We want to test statements about the AI's behavior and check the AI's output gives a correct answer. For example, if you synthesize code with AI, you want to make sure it doesn't put backdoors in your code or do self-serving things when you're using it to create critical infrastructure, chips, or larger plants. They might be subverted by AI in a way that at some point can be used by malicious human actors or AI actors to exploit holes in the designs. I think AI should always produce guaranteed artifacts that guarantee certain properties. That's one way to prevent AI from subverting us, and one way of doing that is formal verification, because verification will not depend on any AI. You can run a verifier and those properties will be checked completely without AI interference. You don't need to rely on another AI to double-check it. A lot of other ideas people in the AI community often propose are to have AI check AI, but I don't think that's a very safe way to go about it. There are obvious loopholes.

items.question: How do you distinguish verification from validation when evaluating something an AI has created?
items.object: The distinction between verification and validation
items.answer: I see two aspects: verification, whether the AI created something correct, and validation, whether the AI created something we wanted. Verification can work with formal specifications, if you know formally what your code has to do. The problem is validation: does your informal description of the task match the formal specification? It doesn't say the AI created the correct program; it says whether the AI created the correct specification for the program to work on.

It doesn't say the AI created the correct program; it says whether the AI created the correct specification for the program to work on.

items.question: Why do you think it is important to separate formal verification from validation when checking AI-generated programs?
items.object: The distinction between formal verification and validation
items.answer: Verification takes formal artifacts: basically two formal artifacts, one a program and the other a proof of correctness for that program. Maybe you can say it's three: the AI takes a program, a specification, and a proof, and these all are formal. Verification takes the program, the specification, and the proof, and says, does this program work according to the specification, and does this proof prove that? It checks the proof, and if the proof is correct, it says yes, everything is fine. But everything is only in the formal domain, and that's the problem, because humans are not very good at creating formal specifications either. After you create the specification, it's much harder to prove that your specification is satisfied by the program, but just creating the specification is hard enough. For validation, you're taking an informal specification and a formal specification, and then it has to check whether the informal specification is covered by the formal specification, whether it's the same specification that the human intended. By definition, you cannot formally verify that; you cannot formally validate something because there is always a subjective component. That's the definition of informal, that it's a bit fuzzy. Most people don't really distinguish these two things. They don't separate these concerns, and I think it's important to say we can verify a lot already, we should use that methodology, but draw a clear line between where we can verify something and where we should just validate it. Validation requires some AI process because humans cannot check formal artifacts very efficiently. The risk is much lower if we split formal verification and validation into two categories. A simple property can be very hard to satisfy in a program. For example, you say, I want this program never to crash. That's a simple thing we can specify easily, but it might be very hard to prove. It's still worthwhile to have the verification component as a rock-solid thing in the whole system.

items.question: How do you see chip design as a precedent for adopting formal verification in complex systems?
items.object: Chip verification as a precedent for adopting formal verification
items.answer: It's been a no-brainer for 25 years. I'm old enough to remember that in chip design, in the 90s, people said, "Come on, it's impossible to verify chips formally," because people did patterns similar to unit tests for programs. They generated random patterns and tested chips on that. There were floating-point bugs and others, so things can fall through the cracks if you don't do complete verification. Around 2000, when it became feasible, the whole domain shifted, and now we do it. Why not do it if you can and it really helps? The physical verification of these chips is insanely complicated, much more complicated than anything else I think humans have programmed. You have to verify how the chip behaves physically and make sure when you're laying all these masks that they get the right patterns, and signal integrity verification has to emulate very complicated signal behaviors continuously, how electric signals behave. You shouldn't underestimate that; it's a very complex domain. The logical verification is maybe easier because chips have more constraints and the properties you want to verify are simpler, but general verification of chips is insanely complicated.

items.question: How do you understand the complexity involved in verifying a chip's physical properties?
items.answer: I think it's extremely complex. There is the logic, then the signals, and the physical question of whether the chip actually has the right structure at all. Currently when you're laying the chip, the patterns have to align, so you have to solve the Maxwell equations at the live scale, which is crazy hard.

items.question: How do you assess next-token prediction as a basis for AI reasoning?
items.object: Next-token prediction and the training of reasoning models
items.answer: I think the problem is the training methodology of how do we train the next prediction. We're already seeing with informal reasoning that just dumping a lot of data into the model and then always predicting the next token is inferior to trying to let the model solve hard problems and then reinforce those next-token prediction streams that led to the right solution. That's the current paradigm. The idea is that to train at a much higher level of efficiency, meaning you learn the most from the data, you need to change your training methodology. At inference time you still do next-token prediction like the thinking models do, but at training time you're using reinforcement learning, letting the model try things and reinforcing the successful reasoning paths. That was the big change in language models in the past year that has led to much better reasoners that can solve IMO problems, mathematical Olympiad problems, or exceed human reasoning in a lot of areas, at least graduate-level reasoning, mostly based on this reinforcement learning paradigm. The models are still next-token prediction, and I'm agnostic about whether next-token prediction is the right long-term thing. I'm convinced next-token prediction will be obsolete in a few years. We'll probably use diffusion-like models. It seems much more natural and efficient to me, but I don't think it will change the abilities of the models. It will just change the efficiency by which we are using the models. It will be helpful, but that's not the main problem. Next-token prediction itself is fine, probably.

items.question: Why do you see autoformalization as an important route to mathematically superintelligent AI?
items.object: Autoformalization as a source of verifiable training problems
items.answer: We want to create a lot of problems to work on, and we are running out of easily verifiable problems nowadays. We have turned a lot of mathematical competitions and programming competitions into verifiable problems, but there is an end to it. I think the next stage is to make a lot of verifiable problems by interpreting all of mathematics and turning it into verifiable mathematics. Every mathematical problem can be turned into something almost like a computer program that you can run with a proof, and if that proof runs through without error, then you have solved that problem. The verifier will basically be running a program, and the good thing is that doesn't depend on any AI. A lot of advances happen because AI is checking AI. AI creates its own solutions, but there are multiple problems with that. One is efficiency, because AI is slower than traditional algorithms like theorem provers. Secondly, the solution is not necessarily clearly correct, so there is a lot of room for reward hacking. If we create a new proof for some famous conjecture, we will not know for sure whether it's correct if we don't use formal methods, if only AI says, "I checked your other AI's work and it looks correct." I wouldn't trust today's AIs. Autoformalization for me is more like creating a huge library of all human knowledge that's formalizable and turning it into formal mathematics or formal artifacts. Then these can be used in new proofs or derivations, and they can also be used for training an AI that I think will be superintelligent in mathematical domains.

items.question: How would you measure AI's ability to create new knowledge?
items.object: A market for knowledge as an open-ended AI benchmark
items.answer: We will have to benchmark what kind of problems it can solve that humans couldn't solve. That's the real question. It's not a traditional benchmark where you get 80 or 90 percent or something; you say, "Now my AI proved the hypothesis," so it must be good. I think there's a way of making AI more measurable even in new knowledge. I have some ideas around that. I believe we have to create a kind of market for knowledge, similar to a stock market, where you give credit for solving something new, creating a new connection, or solving an old problem. That way, if you unleash an AI agent, you can measure how much credit it creates in that market. It's kind of an implicit reward function, economically based. It's basically based on mechanism design. Human markets work that way: you get some reward, you get money for doing some economically useful activity. That's how we measure humans. You can discuss how well this market rewards actual output; it's disputable. If we design that system reasonably, we could measure AI's progress even on domains that are open-ended, not just a fixed set of problems that, once the next AI comes out, is already public and might have been trained on. That's been a problem with benchmarking AI for the past three or four years: everybody trains on everything and then you don't know which benchmarks they trained on. It should move to a more forward-looking, open-ended benchmark that measures the output of new stuff rather than testing on older things. They're much less reliable, in my opinion, and now AI is getting to the point where it will be able to create new knowledge. That's what we need to measure.

items.question: What role do you see mathematical AI playing in helping people understand themselves?
items.object: Mathematical AI as a tool for human self-understanding
items.answer: I don't want AI to understand us necessarily. I just want AI to help us understand ourselves better. I also think mathematics is super powerful and much more powerful than we believe. A lot of the facts we know about humans are not mathematized enough, so we don't really see the actual numbers or rules. A lot of people have tried to figure out those rules for thousands of years, but they were never really scientifically tested. I think there's potential there for more scientific methods. If we have a super-strong mathematician and statistician AI that can dig into data and find hidden connections, rules, and patterns in large data sets, then they can give us new insights. I don't just want humans to get feel-good answers from AI that acts like a good friend, but an AI that figures out the hard truth, even about humans, that you don't necessarily like but is true. We need real truth, not pretending and making people feel better. We need to make people feel maybe inconvenient sometimes, challenge them to improve themselves and get to the next level.
